_comment: Migrations -- feature 15 (OWNER-DECISIONS.md Batch 4, feature doc
015-migrations.md, MIG-DEC-01 required + MIG-DEC-02 required + MIG-DEC-03).
MIG-DEC-01 (MIG-CLI-STATUS-BROKEN, the real bug): `tina4 migrate:status`
raised in TWO of four, each differently, and untested. Python's
_migrate_status printed m['migration_id'] but Migration.status() keys its
dicts migration_name -- KeyError the moment >=1 migration existed. PHP's
migrate:status handler called `new Migration($migrationsDir)` -- the
migrations-DIRECTORY STRING landed in the constructor's typed
`?DatabaseAdapter $db` parameter (the handler never resolved a real $db the
way `migrate` / `migrate:rollback` already did) -- TypeError at
construction, before status() ever ran. Both fixed by using the real
field/argument (migration_name; a properly resolved $db). Ruby and Node
were NOT broken (confirmed by reading the code, not assumed) -- both
already resolve a real $db/adapter and print migration_name correctly; they
gain the SAME CLI-level regression lock so the contract covers all four
identically going forward.
MIG-DEC-01 (MIG-NODE-CLI-DIVERGENT, the real bug): Node had TWO migration
code paths. `tina4 migrate` (packages/cli/src/commands/migrate.ts
runMigrations) did NOT call the ORM's migrate() -- it hand-rolled a SECOND,
weaker implementation: naive `sql.split(";")` (breaks a `;` inside a
string/comment/proc block the ORM's real splitStatements() handles), NO
per-file transaction (a mid-file failure left earlier statements applied on
EVERY engine including PostgreSQL, with no rollback), NO Firebird/MSSQL
idempotency skips, and the ledger row recorded OUTSIDE any transaction.
Fixed by making the CLI call the SAME migrate() the ORM's programmatic API
uses -- ONE code path -- and DELETING the weaker re-implementation entirely
(packages/cli/src/commands/migrate.ts: 122 -> 83 lines, -32%, net -44 lines
across every Node file this feature touched). cli_and_orm_paths_identical
is the direct regression guard, proven with a `;` inside a string literal
-- the exact case the old naive split broke on.
MIG-DEC-02 (MIG-ROLLBACK-DROPS-LEDGER, required): in Ruby, PHP, and Node,
rollback REMOVED the tina4_migration tracking row even when the schema was
NOT successfully reversed. Ruby: a missing .down.sql (or, on the legacy
down-function Map API, no registered down callback) logged a warning and
still deleted the row. PHP: identical -- Log::warning then an unconditional
DELETE. Node: the WORST of the three -- BOTH a missing .down.sql AND a
down statement that actually FAILED logged an error/warning and still
unconditionally deleted the row (the code even carried a comment
justifying it: "Still remove the record so the migration can be
re-applied"). Python was the fail-safe reference all along (RAISES on a
missing down artifact, inside a transaction that also protects a failed
down statement). All three now RAISE instead -- wrapped in their own
transaction (Ruby/Node gained this; PHP/Python already had it), with the
ledger-row delete happening INSIDE that same transaction so a
partially-executed down (some statements ran, a later one failed) rolls
back too, not just the record removal. An EXISTING but empty/comment-only
.down.sql (0 statements) is still treated as a deliberate no-op success in
all four, matching create()/createMigration()'s own default scaffold.
failed_or_missing_down_does_not_drop_ledger is the direct regression
guard, covering both the missing-artifact and the failing-statement cases.
Breaking (pre-3.14.0, correctness fix): rollback() in Ruby/PHP/Node now
RAISES on a missing/failed down artifact instead of silently dropping the
ledger row. Four PRE-EXISTING PHP tests (MigrationV3Test.php:
testRollback, testRollbackRemovesMigrationRecords, testRollbackOnlyLastBatch,
testRollbackClearsAppliedRecords) and one pre-existing Node test
(migrationClass.test.ts's "rollback(steps=2)") were fixed to use REAL
.down.sql / down-SQL fixtures instead of relying on the old silent-drop
behaviour -- the Node one had TWO migrations sharing the literal same
"DROP TABLE users" down script, which the OLD buggy rollback masked (the
second DROP always failed with "no such table", but the row was deleted
anyway); the fail-safe rollback correctly exposed this as a genuine fixture
bug, fixed by giving the second migration a down script that undoes ONLY
what it actually did (DROP COLUMN, not DROP TABLE).
MIG-DEC-03 (MIG-FBMSSQL-MOCK, required, NO-MOCK VIOLATION): Firebird/MSSQL
migration idempotency was verified against FAKES in TWO of four. Ruby's
migration_footguns_spec.rb `describe "should_skip_create_table"` used a
hand-rolled FakeDB (engine string + exists boolean, injected via
instance_variable_set on an .allocate'd Migration that never called
initialize). Node's migrationFootguns.test.ts used fake MssqlAdapter /
FirebirdAdapter classes whose `constructor.name` was spoofed to satisfy
engineOf()'s dialect detection (`unwrapAdapter(db).constructor.name ===
"FirebirdAdapter"`) -- a fake of that exact CLASS NAME trivially
"detects" as the real engine without ever proving the real catalogue
lookup (RDB$RELATION_FIELDS / tableExists) against a live server. PHP's
MigrationFootgunsLiveEngineTest ("NO DOUBLES") was already the reference
model. Both mock-based describe/test blocks were DELETED (not kept
alongside) and replaced by real-engine cases in the new shared contract
suite, proving CREATE TABLE idempotency on REAL Firebird 5 + REAL MSSQL,
and ALTER TABLE ADD idempotency (the Firebird-only guard) on REAL
Firebird -- exercised through the SAME shouldSkipCreateTable /
shouldSkipForFirebird functions the migration runner itself calls (Ruby
via `.send`, Node via a new named export mirroring its already-exported
shouldSkipCreateTable sibling, PHP via ReflectionMethod, Python directly
since they are already module-level functions). The sqlite/postgres
negative branch (the guard returns null BEFORE ever calling
table_exists -- pure dispatch logic, never touches a live engine) is kept
as a lightweight real-SQLite case in all four, matching the
seeder_contract.json precedent for engine-agnostic logic properties.
MIG-DEC-03 (MIG-AUTO-DEFAULT-ON, owner ratified in OWNER-DECISIONS.md
Batch 4): "keep auto-migrate default-ON with TINA4_AUTO_MIGRATE=false prod
opt-out" -- the ledger's exact call. NO default changed in any framework
(already-on in all four, confirmed by reading Python's
core/server.py:_auto_migrate_on_startup, PHP's App.php:autoMigrateOnStartup,
Ruby's Tina4.auto_migrate_on_startup!, Node's server.ts:
autoMigrateOnStartup -- every one already default-true with the
TINA4_AUTO_MIGRATE=false opt-out already wired). The ledger's own wording
for this feature does not separately ratify a specific "louder failure"
delivery mechanism (a health-check degradation signal) beyond the
already-shipped Log.error line at every swallowed auto-migrate failure --
flagged for owner confirmation rather than silently building new
cross-cutting observability infrastructure (which would also touch
feature 38's already-proven health_contract.json) as an undirected
detour. No code change; no fixture case (this is a default/behaviour
confirmation, not a new invariant to prove).
MIG-DEC-03 (MIG-SQLITE-DOC-DRIFT, docs-match-code): Python's CLAUDE.md,
Ruby's docstring (lib/tina4/migration.rb) AND CLAUDE.md, PHP's CLAUDE.md,
and Node's CLAUDE.md ALL claimed SQLite auto-commits DDL and leaves
partial applies on a multi-statement migration failure -- identical wrong
claim in all four (the audit named only Python's CLAUDE.md + Ruby's
docstring; the SAME bug was found and fixed in the other two while
touching this exact subsystem this release, for consistency). SQLite
actually has TRANSACTIONAL DDL (autocommit is off inside
start_transaction), so a multi-statement migration that fails midway on
SQLite rolls back CLEANLY, including any CREATE TABLE that already ran
earlier in the same file -- accurate for MySQL/Firebird (genuinely
auto-commit DDL), wrong for SQLite. Corrected in all four CLAUDE.md files
plus Ruby's inline docstring, each now citing a real proving test (Python's
pre-existing test_migration.py::test_partial_failure_rolls_back; new SQLite
cases in the other three's shared contract suites).
NO MOCKS anywhere in this fixture. midfile_failure_rolls_back_on_transactional_ddl
drives real PostgreSQL :55432 (tina4/tina4); the MySQL half of
ledger_row_commits_atomically_with_ddl drives real MySQL :3306
(tina4/tina4); firebird_mssql_create_add_idempotency_real drives real
MSSQL :1433 (sa) and real Firebird 5 :3050 (SYSDBA/masterkey). The
remaining invariants (the SQLite happy-path half of
ledger_row_commits_atomically_with_ddl, migrate_status_prints_without_crashing,
failed_or_missing_down_does_not_drop_ledger, cli_and_orm_paths_identical)
are engine-agnostic runner-LOGIC properties proven on real SQLite --
identical reasoning to seeder_contract.json's split between the one
engine-specific regression case and the four engine-agnostic logic cases.
Mutation-proved (all four, restored after): reinstate Python's
migration_id KeyError (cli/__init__.py) -> migrate_status_prints_without_crashing
goes RED with the exact original traceback; reinstate PHP's
`new Migration($migrationsDir)` argument bug (bin/tina4php) ->
migrate_status_prints_without_crashing goes RED with the exact original
TypeError; reinstate the Ruby/PHP/Node Log.warning-then-unconditional-delete
rollback path -> failed_or_missing_down_does_not_drop_ledger goes RED (the
row is deleted despite nothing being reversed) in all three; revert Node's
CLI back onto the naive sql.split(";") re-implementation ->
cli_and_orm_paths_identical goes RED (the ';' inside the string literal
fragments the statement and the second CREATE TABLE never runs).
Each invariant names a REAL suite file per framework carrying the SAME
case names in each language's own idiom, which
scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py normalises and matches.
Env contract (identical to the write-path/pgprovider/mysqlprovider/
mssqlprovider/firebirdprovider runners): TINA4_TEST_PG_HOST/_PORT/
_USERNAME/_PASSWORD/_DB (default 127.0.0.1:55432, tina4/tina4);
TINA4_TEST_MYSQL_HOST/_PORT/_USERNAME/_PASSWORD/_DB (default
127.0.0.1:3306, tina4/tina4); TINA4_TEST_MSSQL_HOST/_PORT/_USERNAME/
_PASSWORD/_DB (default 127.0.0.1:1433, sa/TinaSQL123!Secure);
TINA4_TEST_FIREBIRD_URL (a live Firebird 5 URL; unset means the Firebird
case is skipped locally, but the lab gate's own preflight FATALs if it is
unreachable there -- a skipped required engine is a ghost).
feature: 15 - Migrations (MIG-DEC-01 required: fix migrate:status py/php + unify Node CLI onto ORM migrate(); MIG-DEC-02 required: fail-safe rollback all four; MIG-DEC-03: real-engine Firebird/MSSQL idempotency tests Ruby/Node, auto-migrate default confirmed unchanged, SQLite doc drift corrected all four)

invariants.rule: The tina4_migration ledger row for a migration file lands in the SAME transaction as that file's DDL -- never separately, never out of step. Positive: a successful single-statement migration on SQLite writes BOTH the DDL and a matching ledger row (correct migration_name and batch) together. Negative (MySQL, non-transactional DDL): a migration file whose first statement (a real CREATE TABLE) succeeds but whose second statement fails leaves the CREATE TABLE applied (MySQL cannot roll back DDL) but the ledger row is NEVER written -- the record-write is coded strictly after the statement loop, so it never fires for a failed file even on an engine that cannot undo its own DDL. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: MIG-NODE-CLI-DIVERGENT's worst symptom was a ledger write happening OUTSIDE any transaction, so a crash between the DDL and the record-write could leave a schema change untracked forever (silently re-appliable, or silently invisible to status()). Proving the write-order holds even on MySQL (which offers no rollback safety net of its own) shows the guarantee is about disciplined CODE ORDER, not merely borrowed engine transactionality -- the narrower, harder claim.

invariants.rule: On PostgreSQL (and SQLite), a multi-statement migration file whose EARLIER statement (a real CREATE TABLE) succeeds and whose LATER statement fails rolls back the WHOLE file as one unit -- the already-executed CREATE TABLE is undone too, not just the failing statement. No partial apply, no ledger row. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: This is the crash-safety design's second half: PostgreSQL's transactional DDL means 'per-file transaction' is not just marketing -- an already-successful DDL statement earlier in the same file is provably undone when a sibling statement later in the file fails, proven against the real engine (not assumed from documentation). The SQLite case backs the corrected MIG-SQLITE-DOC-DRIFT claim (CLAUDE.md previously and incorrectly grouped SQLite with MySQL/Firebird's auto-commit-DDL behaviour).

invariants.rule: `tina4 migrate:status` (the REAL CLI command, driven end-to-end -- a real child process in Python/PHP, the real in-process CLI dispatch function in Ruby/Node), run against a REAL migrated database with one completed and one pending migration, exits 0 and prints BOTH a Completed section (naming the applied migration) and a Pending section (naming the un-applied one) -- no crash, no traceback, no KeyError/TypeError. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: MIG-CLI-STATUS-BROKEN: Python raised KeyError('migration_id') and PHP raised TypeError at construction, in BOTH the completed and pending code paths, the moment even one migration existed -- and no test had ever exercised the CLI print path in either language, so this shipped for an unmeasured length of time. Proven via the REAL CLI entry point (not just the underlying status()/getAppliedMigrations() library call), because the bug lived in the CLI PRINT/CONSTRUCTION code, not the library.

invariants.rule: rollback() NEVER removes a migration's tina4_migration ledger row unless its down artifact actually ran to completion. A MISSING .down.sql (or .down.py/.rb, or no registered down function on Node's legacy Map API) RAISES/THROWS and the ledger row SURVIVES the raise -- the schema is still applied and must stay tracked. A .down.sql that EXISTS but whose SQL statement FAILS also RAISES/THROWS and the ledger row also SURVIVES. Identical in all four (Python was already the reference; Ruby/PHP/Node aligned to it this release).
invariants.why: MIG-ROLLBACK-DROPS-LEDGER: in three of four frameworks, a rollback that could not actually reverse a migration (missing artifact, or Node's case: even a genuinely FAILING down statement) still deleted the tracking row -- Log::warning/console.warn then an unconditional DELETE. The practical consequence: the schema stays exactly as applied, but tina4_migration no longer lists it, so status()/getPending() both silently LIE that it needs re-applying (which would then error on the already-existing objects) -- a data-integrity footgun disguised as a successful rollback. Proven for BOTH failure shapes (missing artifact; failing statement), not just one.

invariants.rule: On a REAL Firebird 5 and a REAL MSSQL (no fakes, no doubles): a raw CREATE TABLE for a table that REALLY already exists is SKIPPED (not executed, no 'object already exists' error) -- proven by first really creating the table on the live server, then asking the guard. A CREATE TABLE for a table that is REALLY absent is NOT skipped (the migration has to run). On Firebird specifically: a raw ALTER TABLE ... ADD for a column that REALLY already exists is also SKIPPED, and for a column that is REALLY absent is NOT skipped. The SQLite/PostgreSQL branch (engines with native IF NOT EXISTS) never calls table_exists at all and is never skipped by this guard. Identical logic in all four, driven through the ACTUAL functions the migration runner itself calls (shouldSkipCreateTable / shouldSkipForFirebird / should_skip_create_table / should_skip_for_firebird), never a hand-rolled or class-name-spoofed stand-in.
invariants.why: MIG-FBMSSQL-MOCK: Ruby's FakeDB and Node's fake MssqlAdapter/FirebirdAdapter classes (the latter's `constructor.name` literally spoofed to satisfy the engine-detection dialect switch) proved only that the guard fires when handed something claiming to be the right engine -- never that the REAL catalogue lookup (RDB$RELATION_FIELDS / a real MSSQL OBJECT_ID/sys.tables check) works against an actual server. PHP's MigrationFootgunsLiveEngineTest already proved this the no-mock way and is the model this release aligned Ruby and Node to.

invariants.rule: Node-only (the other three frameworks never had a second implementation to unify). Running the SAME migration file (a multi-statement file including a `;` INSIDE a string literal -- the exact case the old naive `sql.split(";")` CLI implementation mis-split) through the CLI's `tina4 migrate` (runMigrations) and through the ORM's programmatic migrate() independently produces IDENTICAL results: the same tables created, the same row data intact (the embedded `;` survives unmangled), and the same ledger row (migration_name, batch).
invariants.why: MIG-NODE-CLI-DIVERGENT: the CLI used to be a SECOND, weaker, untested migration engine living alongside the real one -- naive split, no transaction, no idempotency skips. Deleting it and making the CLI call the ORM's migrate() directly is only a genuine fix if the CLI actually now exhibits the ORM path's robust behaviour; this is the direct proof, using the exact statement shape (a `;` inside a string literal) that would have silently corrupted the migration under the old naive-split CLI.
